title: Hitchhiking Across China: Thumbs Up Season 3 (Part 1/5)
summary: Season Three begins in Beijing with David preparing for a China exhibition, describing explicit sources for his paintings and recruiting Mia and Stephanie before beginning the trip with Harry. Stephanie is a participant and language broker, not merely a translator or sexual prop. Private drivers and local participants remain unidentified beyond VICE's scene labels. A bus ride reaches Badaling, where David depicts his long-held wish by marking one Great Wall brick; the episode does not establish permission or legality. Restaurant touching, sexual jokes, illness, property marking and purported aphrodisiac claims require literal transcript plus separate consent, safety and attribution context. Chinese speech remains unresolved unless a native-language pass verifies it. Every source idea is preserved; speaker names remain exact publisher-caption provenance only.

connections.why: The road format moves from North America to China.
The season begins with an exhibition and studio rather than the roadside.
David explicitly ties uncomfortable sexual behavior to paintings instead of letting a later archive interpretation invent the link.
Mia says the show's hitchhiking premise is not customary in China.
Stephanie joins as Harry's sister and traveler while also bridging languages.
The first ride introduces the season-long need to retain scenes without resolving strangers' identities.
The exhibition context turns into David's one-sided account of being removed by a gallery.
David repeatedly reframes Stephanie's practical participation as sexual leverage.
Harry's performances continue the series' exchange of art for rides and connection.
David retracts his assumption that a bus passenger is angry; both claims belong together.
Chinese speech cannot be reconstructed from surrounding English banter.
A painting fantasy becomes physical marking of cultural heritage without demonstrated permission.
Stephanie corrects David rather than serving as a frictionless narrator.
The season again makes Harry's body and performance a spectacle, now through David's Buddha framing.
David's instruction to kiss a woman cannot stand in for either person's agreement or an event.
Datong is reached, while Mongolia and the Yellow River remain planning language.
David's illness mirrors earlier seasons' recurring bodily consequences without proving a diagnosis.
Stephanie's language work is immediately surrounded by David's sexual commentary.
David again appears to exchange painting for hospitality, but object and permission need video verification.
Translated or improvised claims about sexual effects of food must not become factual archive metadata.

source_notes.claim: Badaling is a Great Wall location.
source_notes.assessment: Badaling is a recognized section of the Great Wall. The episode's marking scene still requires its own permission and conservation context.

source_notes.claim: David has the flu because he reports diarrhea and feeling ill.
source_notes.assessment: This is David's self-diagnosis. Gastrointestinal symptoms have many causes; preserve his words without converting them into a medical finding.

source_notes.claim: Nine speaker categories occur in the manual captions.
source_notes.assessment: VICE supplies exact-span labels for David Choe, Harry Kim, Mia, Stephanie, Mr. Huang, Mr. Zhao, Mr. Xi and generic male/female speakers. None is credited to an acoustic model.

speaker_policy.status: publisher labels retained; model-generated named turns withheld
speaker_policy.reason: Exact manual-caption prefixes are candidates with acoustic_verified=false. Labels never propagate to adjacent unlabeled spans. Mia, Stephanie and all private local participants are excluded from durable voice/face identity claims until independently listening-verified and policy-eligible; private strangers remain excluded from enrollment. Chinese-language identity and translation cannot be inferred from neighboring English captions.

publication_restrictions.rule: Preserve every source idea and literal wording; corrections and context remain separate.
Publisher speaker labels are exact-span provenance only, never acoustic-model output.
Do not propagate a label across unlabeled speech or infer a speaker from adjacency.
Keep exhibition chronology attributed until independent records verify it.
Do not sanitize explicit autobiography or extract it as decontextualized promotional copy.
Do not infer Mia's private identity, contact trail or relationship beyond the episode.
Do not reduce Stephanie to translator, sexual leverage or a voice-enrollment target.
Do not invent Chinese translations or claim fluency from the edited episode.
No face, plate, route, employer, ethnicity or identity search for private drivers.
Do not geolocate the gallery/building/camp or assert property rights absent evidence.
Do not turn roadside/freeway scenes into route or evasion instructions.
Keep Stephanie's participation and David's objectification distinct; narration is not consent.
Music/performance cues require rights and exact-work verification before reuse.
Keep David's retraction adjacent to his unsupported reading of a private woman.
All Chinese-language spans remain unresolved until native-language listening review.
Describe only what the episode depicts/claims; do not celebrate, instruct, legalize or criminalize the Great Wall marking without evidence.
Do not use Buddha/body framing as participant belief, ethnicity metadata, thumbnail text or archive voice.
No face extraction or consent inference for restaurant participants.
Distinguish reached places from proposed destinations and subjective regional language.
Do not identify repair workers, shop or location from visual clues.
Do not diagnose David or create medical profiles for participants.
Huang, Zhao and Xi remain scene-only publisher labels; no surname expansion or notable-person linking.
Do not infer what was painted, ownership or permission without video review.
Never publish food/sexual-potency banter as medical, sexual-health or nutrition guidance.
